Price and Quantity Indices

Source: R/priceIndex.R
priceIndex.Rd

Bilateral index numbers comparing prices (or quantities) of a set of items between a base period 0 and a comparison period 1. The unweighted (elementary) indices need prices only, the weighted ones use quantities to weight the items by their economic importance.

Usage

priceIndex(
  p0,
  p1,
  q0 = NULL,
  q1 = NULL,
  estimator = c("laspeyres", "paasche", "fisher", "tornqvist", "walsh",
    "marshall-edgeworth", "drobisch", "sato-vartia", "geo-laspeyres", "geo-paasche",
    "palgrave", "jevons", "carli", "dutot"),
  na.rm = FALSE
)

quantityIndex(
  q0,
  q1,
  p0 = NULL,
  p1 = NULL,
  estimator = c("laspeyres", "paasche", "fisher", "tornqvist", "walsh",
    "marshall-edgeworth", "drobisch", "sato-vartia", "geo-laspeyres", "geo-paasche",
    "palgrave", "jevons", "carli", "dutot"),
  na.rm = FALSE
)

Arguments

p0, p1

numeric vectors of prices in the base and in the comparison period. Must be non-negative, and strictly positive for estimators built on price relatives.

q0, q1

numeric vectors of non-negative quantities in the base and in the comparison period, or NULL where the estimator does not need them

estimator

the index formula, see Details

na.rm

logical, should items with a missing price or quantity be removed? Defaults to FALSE, in which case the result is NA as soon as one value used by the estimator is missing.

Value

A single unnamed numeric value, the index as a ratio (1 = no change). NA if no items are left or if the index is not defined, e.g. for a basket without any expenditure.

Details

All vectors are matched by position: element i of p0, p1, q0 and q1 must refer to the same item. For panels in long format, with items entering and leaving over time, see chainedIndex().

Writing \(r_i = p_{i1}/p_{i0}\) for the price relatives and \(s_{it} = p_{it} q_{it} / \sum_j p_{jt} q_{jt}\) for the expenditure shares, the estimators are:

"laspeyres"

\(\sum p_1 q_0 / \sum p_0 q_0\), base period basket

"paasche"

\(\sum p_1 q_1 / \sum p_0 q_1\), comparison period basket

"fisher"

geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche

"drobisch"

arithmetic mean of Laspeyres and Paasche

"marshall-edgeworth"

basket \(q_0 + q_1\)

"walsh"

basket \(\sqrt{q_0 q_1}\)

"tornqvist"

\(\prod r_i^{(s_{i0} + s_{i1})/2}\)

"sato-vartia"

\(\prod r_i^{w_i}\) with weights proportional to the logarithmic mean of \(s_{i0}\) and \(s_{i1}\)

"geo-laspeyres"

\(\prod r_i^{s_{i0}}\)

"geo-paasche"

\(\prod r_i^{s_{i1}}\)

"palgrave"

\(\sum s_{i1} r_i\)

"jevons"

unweighted geometric mean of the price relatives

"carli"

unweighted arithmetic mean of the price relatives

"dutot"

ratio of the unweighted mean prices, \(\sum p_1 / \sum p_0\)

Fisher, Walsh and Törnqvist are superlative indices (Diewert, 1976) and usually agree closely; Laspeyres and Paasche bracket them in the typical case of substitution towards items that became relatively cheaper. Fisher and Sato-Vartia satisfy the factor reversal test: the product of the price and the quantity index equals the ratio of total expenditure.

All weighted indices are invariant to the scale of the quantities, i.e. to the size of the population the quantities were observed in. With the exception of "marshall-edgeworth" this also holds if the scale differs between the two periods.

Estimators that use only one basket need only that basket: "laspeyres" and "geo-laspeyres" work without q1, "paasche", "geo-paasche" and "palgrave" without q0. Quantities supplied but not used by the chosen estimator are ignored.

quantityIndex() is the same set of formulas with the roles of prices and quantities interchanged.

References

Balk, B. M. (2008). Price and Quantity Index Numbers: Models for Measuring Aggregate Change and Difference. Cambridge University Press.

Diewert, W. E. (1976). Exact and superlative index numbers. Journal of Econometrics, 4(2), 115–145.

ILO, IMF, OECD, UNECE, Eurostat and World Bank (2004). Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice. International Labour Office, Geneva.

See also

chainedIndex() for chained indices over several periods

Other index.price: chainedIndex()

Examples

p0 <- c(2.0, 5.0, 10.0)
p1 <- c(2.2, 5.5, 9.0)
q0 <- c(100, 40, 10)
q1 <- c(90, 45, 14)

priceIndex(p0, p1, q0)
#> [1] 1.06
## [1] 1.06
priceIndex(p0, p1, q0, q1, estimator = "paasche")
#> [1] 1.048624
## [1] 1.048624
priceIndex(p0, p1, q0, q1, estimator = "tornqvist")
#> [1] 1.054558
## [1] 1.054558
priceIndex(p0, p1, estimator = "jevons")
#> [1] 1.028828
## [1] 1.028828

# factor reversal: price index x quantity index = expenditure ratio
priceIndex(p0, p1, q0, q1, estimator = "fisher") *
  quantityIndex(q0, q1, p0, p1, estimator = "fisher")
#> [1] 1.143
## [1] 1.143
sum(p1 * q1) / sum(p0 * q0)
#> [1] 1.143
## [1] 1.143
